I'm Dilnaz, and I sit behind Zeenat in class, so I saw her smiling at her phone all week. On Thursday she turned around. "Promise not to laugh? I've been chatting with a boy from my game group for two months. He wants to meet on Sunday at the old bus stand." She sounded excited and jittery at once, twisting the end of her dupatta.
I asked if her parents knew. "No, he said they wouldn't get it." I couldn't tell whether she believed that or just wanted to. I told her that line bothered me.
She was quiet, then said the line bothered her too. That night she showed her mother the chats. On Friday she told me her mother had said there would be no meeting, and they had blocked and reported him together. "If he wanted to meet me properly, he wouldn't need me to hide it," she said.

qa.q: Where did the boy want Zeenat to meet him?
qa.a: At the old bus stand on Sunday.

qa.q: What did Zeenat seem to be feeling when she told Dilnaz about the meeting?
qa.a: She sounded excited and jittery at once and twisted the end of her dupatta, though Dilnaz couldn't be sure what she truly believed.

qa.q: Which choice kept Zeenat safe once the secrecy line came up, and why?
qa.a: She showed her mother the chats, and her mother decided there would be no meeting; they blocked and reported him, because a contact who wants parents kept out is a warning sign.

qa.q: Why did the line "they wouldn't get it" bother Dilnaz?
qa.a: Dilnaz saw it as a way of keeping parents out, and secrecy from parents is a warning sign, so Dilnaz worried about Zeenat's safety.

grounding: Shows a teen curious to meet an online friend who stays cautious, tells a parent and steps back once the contact pushes secrecy, so no meeting happens.

passage:
Jaya waited in the school corridor outside the counsellor's room until the bell had stopped ringing. Inside, Gautam, the counsellor, let her sit without speaking for a minute.
Then she said, "I sent money from Ma's account to someone who promised me a phone. It's gone." Her voice cracked. "Ma will be so angry. Papa too. I can't say it."
Gautam nodded slowly. "That sounds heavy. Most parents would rather hear the truth than find out later, and the sooner they know, the more can be done, like calling the bank. I can sit with you when you tell them."
Jaya looked at the floor, then nodded. That evening Gautam phoned her mother, and Jaya, sitting beside him, took the phone for the last part.

qa.q: What had Jaya been promised in return for the money?
qa.a: She had been promised a phone.

qa.q: Why did Jaya find it hard to say what happened?
qa.a: She fears that Ma will be angry, and Papa too, and she feels ashamed, so her voice cracked.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do to help Jaya tell her parents?
qa.a: Gautam let her sit quietly, explained that most parents prefer the truth and that quick action can limit the damage, and offered to sit with her when she tells them. 🤍

qa.q: How might Jaya's mother feel when she hears?
qa.a: She may feel shock and worry about the money, but probably more concern for her daughter, who came forward instead of hiding it.

grounding: Shows a teen afraid to tell her parents about a scam, encouraged by a counsellor to tell early.

passage:
I'm Nakul, and I was on the sofa while my cousin Mridul played online in our flat. He kept grinning at the screen. "An older player gave me a rare skin for free. He says I'm the best he's met, and I should add him on a private chat."
Then Mridul hesitated. "He also said not to tell my parents, because they'd make me stop." His grin dropped a little.
I asked, "Why would a grown-up give free stuff to a kid and want it kept secret?" He shrugged and said the skin was cool, but he didn't look sure.
Later I saw him remove the friend request. At dinner he told his mother. She put down her spoon, thanked him for telling her and said it wasn't his fault. They blocked and reported the account together that evening. I don't know whether he was scared or just tired of it.

qa.q: What did the older player give Mridul for free?
qa.a: He gave Mridul a rare skin.

qa.q: What did Mridul seem to be feeling when he hesitated?
qa.a: His grin dropped a little and he didn't look sure, so he seemed uneasy about the gift and the secrecy, though Nakul can't know for certain.

qa.q: What could Mridul do when someone offers gifts that come with secrecy?
qa.a: He can refuse gifts that come with secrecy, remove the contact and tell his parents or another trusted adult, as he did at dinner.

qa.q: How did Mridul's mother react when he told her at dinner?
qa.a: She stayed calm, thanked him for telling her and said it wasn't his fault, then blocked and reported the account with him that same evening.

grounding: Shows a teen offered gifts by an older gaming contact who asks for secrecy, and choosing to refuse and tell his mother.

passage:
I'm Gurpreet. On Monday morning our class group filled up with an edited photo of Madhuri's face stuck on a cartoon buffalo, and people were forwarding it with laughing faces. Madhuri walked in, saw phones being tucked away, and stopped at the door. Her face went pale and she sat down without a word.
At lunch she didn't eat. When I asked, she only said, "Whatever."
I sat next to her and asked if she wanted to take screenshots. She did. We blocked the account that started it, and she showed the pages to our class teacher. Madhuri never replied with a meme of her own. Later she told me she had felt hurt and exposed, and that saying it out loud helped. The teacher closed the group.

qa.q: What was Madhuri's face edited onto in the photo?
qa.a: It was edited onto a cartoon buffalo.

qa.q: What was Madhuri probably feeling when she walked in and saw phones being tucked away?
qa.a: She likely felt hurt and exposed, since her face went pale and she stopped at the door, and later she said so herself. 🤍

qa.q: What did Madhuri and Gurpreet do that avoided retaliation?
qa.a: They took screenshots, blocked the account that started it and showed the class teacher, instead of replying with another meme.

qa.q: How might the class teacher see the situation?
qa.a: The teacher probably sees a hurt student and a class group being misused, and takes it seriously because Madhuri came with the screenshots.

grounding: Shows a teen mocked with edited images who saves screenshots, blocks, tells a trusted adult and does not retaliate.

The messages came at night, from an account with no photo and a string of numbers for a name. "Nobody likes you." "Quit the choir." Binita read each one twice in her room in Guwahati, and by midnight she had a list: the girl who lost the solo, the boy who mocked her accent, her old lab partner. She couldn't eat or study; the guessing consumed her.
On the phone, Divyansh said, "It doesn't matter who it is right now. Save everything. Screenshot the lot."
In the morning they showed the pages to the choir teacher, reported the account to the app, and the teacher told the school. Binita felt lighter for the first time in days. She still glanced at people, wondering, but she pushed the list into a drawer.

qa.q: Which three people were on Binita's list?
qa.a: The list had the girl who lost the solo, the boy who mocked her accent and her old lab partner.

qa.q: Why couldn't Binita eat or study that night?
qa.a: The guessing about who sent the messages consumed her and the hurtful words kept replaying, so she felt anxious and hurt.

qa.q: What steps did Binita and Divyansh take, and why did they matter?
qa.a: They saved screenshots, reported the account to the app and told the choir teacher, who told the school; this keeps evidence and brings adults in, so Binita doesn't have to solve the puzzle alone.

qa.q: How might Divyansh see Binita's list of suspects?
qa.a: Divyansh probably sees a worried friend spiralling, and believes that saving evidence and reporting matter more than knowing who it is.

grounding: Shows a teen receiving anonymous nasty messages, obsessing over who, then preserving evidence and reporting.

I'm Bidisha, and I was in the plans chat when Nazia's name simply vanished from it. On Friday the others were talking about a picnic at the lake, and Nazia sat two desks away, unpacking her books slowly, glancing at everyone's phones.
I don't know exactly what she felt, but at lunch she said, "I guess I wasn't invited." Her voice was flat. I told her I hadn't known, and that I was sorry. She shrugged.
The next week she started sitting with Amira from the library club, and I saw her laugh. One evening she told her mother, who said to come back if it kept happening. Nazia told me it still stung, but she wasn't on her own.

qa.q: Where were the others planning a picnic?
qa.a: They were planning a picnic at the lake.

qa.q: How can you tell Nazia felt rejected?
qa.a: She glanced at everyone's phones, said "I guess I wasn't invited" in a flat voice, and later said it still stung, though Bidisha can't know exactly what she felt.

qa.q: What did Nazia do that helped after being left out?
qa.a: She found other friends, sitting with Amira from the library club, and told her mother, who said to come back if it kept happening.

qa.q: How might Bidisha feel about having stayed in the chat?
qa.a: Bidisha may feel uneasy or guilty, having told Nazia about not knowing and being sorry, though Bidisha can't fix it alone.

grounding: Shows a teen removed from a group chat and left out, feeling rejected, finding other friends and telling an adult.

passage:
Monday: A fake account posted Chandrika's old photo with a cruel caption, and forty people laughed. Her hands shook. She typed a reply about the bully's family that she was sure would sting, her thumb over the button.
Tuesday: Amandeep found her by the water cooler. "Don't send it. They'll screenshot you and then you're the one in trouble." She didn't answer, but she deleted the draft, hot-faced. "I still want to hurt them," she admitted. "Of course you do," Amandeep said. "That's human." They gathered screenshots and dates instead.
The following Monday: They gave the file to the vice-principal, who took the account down and spoke to the students involved. Chandrika still felt anger sometimes, but she felt steadier.

qa.q: How many people laughed at the fake account's post?
qa.a: Forty people laughed.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when she typed the reply, and what did she admit on Tuesday?
qa.a: She was shaking with anger and wanted the reply to sting; on Tuesday she admitted she still wanted to hurt them.

qa.q: Why was gathering screenshots and dates a better choice than the reply?
qa.a: Evidence can be handed to the school to act on, while a cruel reply could be screenshotted and turn the trouble onto Chandrika herself.

qa.q: How might the vice-principal see Chandrika's file?
qa.a: The vice-principal would see clear evidence and a student who chose to report rather than retaliate, and can act on it fairly.

grounding: Shows a teen wanting to retaliate against a bully, recognising the urge, and choosing evidence and reporting.

passage:
Every morning in the small hill town of Champhai, Damini stood at the school gate with her bag and her stomach clenched. The class chat had a post about her, and it felt as if the whole school had seen it. Twice that week she told her family she felt unwell.
On Thursday her friend Lalremsiami walked her home. "Is it the chat?" Damini nodded, eyes wet. "I think school scares me," she whispered, "and it feels silly."
"It isn't silly. Your fear is telling you something is wrong."
That night Damini showed her mother the phone. The next day they met the headmistress, who promised to look into the post and speak to the class. Damini walked in with her shoulders a little lower.

qa.q: When did Lalremsiami walk Damini home?
qa.a: Lalremsiami walked her home on Thursday.

qa.q: Why did Damini stand at the school gate with her stomach clenched?
qa.a: She dreads school because of the post about her in the class chat, and feels as if the whole school has seen it.

qa.q: What helped Damini deal with her fear?
qa.a: She told her friend and then her mother, and together they asked the headmistress to act, treating the fear as a signal rather than a weakness.

qa.q: How might the headmistress see the situation?
qa.a: The headmistress hears a student who is afraid to come to school because of a post, and sees it as the school's job to act, which is why she promised to look into it and speak to the class.

grounding: Shows a teen dreading school because of what is online, treating fear as a signal and asking adults and the school to act.

passage:
On the bus ride to school in a Himachal hill town, Yash scrolled past the post: a classmate's torn bag, captioned with a joke, already shared a hundred times. He didn't laugh and he didn't say anything. He just kept scrolling.
All evening the picture came back to him. At home his cousin Aadhya asked, "Why so quiet?" "I saw something and did nothing," he said.
"That's guilt," Aadhya said. "What can you do about it now?"
Next morning Yash reported the post, wrote to the classmate, "Hope you're okay. I'm sorry I said nothing," and didn't forward the picture to anyone. The classmate replied with a small thumbs-up, and the knot in his stomach loosened a little.

qa.q: How many times had the post already been shared?
qa.a: It had already been shared a hundred times.

qa.q: Why did the picture keep coming back to Yash all evening?
qa.a: He felt guilty for having seen the post and done nothing about it. 🤍

qa.q: What did Yash do next that turned guilt into action?
qa.a: He reported the post, wrote a kind message to the classmate and refused to forward the picture.

qa.q: How might the classmate feel on receiving Yash's message?
qa.a: The classmate may feel a bit less alone, as the small thumbs-up suggests, even though the mockery still hurt.

grounding: Shows a teen bystander feeling guilty about a mocking post and reporting it, checking on the target and refusing to share.

I'm Arnab, and I was at the next table when Gopika laughed and showed me the sticker she had made from Riya's blurry photo. "It's just a joke," she said. By evening it was in three groups, and someone had added a nasty caption. The next day Riya wasn't at school.
Gopika went quiet, her tea untouched. "I didn't mean it to go that far," she said. Honestly, I said nothing helpful.
Then she took out her phone, deleted the sticker, and asked the group admins to delete it too. The day after, she walked to Riya's seat. "I made that. It was cruel, and I'm sorry. I've taken it down." She didn't say "joke" even once. Riya said she'd think about it, and Gopika nodded.

qa.q: How many groups had the sticker reached by evening?
qa.a: It had reached three groups.

qa.q: What might Gopika have been feeling when she said she didn't mean it to go that far?
qa.a: She seemed shaken and guilty about how far it went, since she went quiet with her tea untouched, though Arnab can't see fully inside her.

qa.q: What did Gopika do to repair the harm, and what did she avoid?
qa.a: She deleted the sticker, asked the admins to delete it too, apologised plainly to Riya and avoided saying it was a joke.

qa.q: How might Riya feel about the apology?
qa.a: Riya may feel some relief but still be hurt, which would explain why she said she would think about it.

grounding: Shows a teen who joined a joke that hurt someone owning it, deleting it and apologising plainly.
